primary_readings.reading_scope: Author identity and legal-history remit checked, including the two Cambridge books, the coedited volume with Richard J. Ross, and the separate coauthorship of Rage for Order with Lisa Ford. Used for identity and credit, not for a career chronology, life dates or the arguments of unread books. No external identifier assigned.

Official Cambridge title, author, volume, issue, pages, July 1999 print metadata and abstract checked. The article body was not read. The new substantive accounts of jurisdictional politics use the separately read 2002 book excerpt, not an implied reading of this article.

Official ten-page chapter excerpt read in full, printed pp. 1–10: multisided legal contests pp. 1–3; institutional world history pp. 3–7; legal-system boundaries and state-centered narratives pp. 8–10. Book remainder unread. Copyright leaf visually checked in https://assets.cambridge.org/97805218/04141/frontmatter/9780521804141_frontmatter.pdf (PDF p. 4): copyright 2002, First published 2002, reprints 2003/2005 and digital printing 2007; hardback ISBN 9780521804141 and paperback 9780521009263. Cambridge Core https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/law-and-colonial-cultures/5DE1BB3C38E1F258F57ACC6A437BACF2 lists 3 December 2001 for print formats and 18 December 2009 online. The chronology follows the examined edition’s explicit first-publication statement, retaining the earlier platform release date as a separate observation rather than declaring it impossible. Acknowledgments p. xi explicitly credit Philip Curtin’s world-history training; no additional lineage edge is inferred.

Read chapter 1 printed pp. 1–5 and 7–10; p. 6 not used for a new claim in this packet. Corridors/enclaves pp. 2–3, divisible authority pp. 3–5, geographic conventions pp. 7–9 and mapping discussion p. 10 support bounded paraphrases. Later chapters unread. Front matter https://assets.cambridge.org/97805218/81050/frontmatter/9780521881050_frontmatter.pdf: copyright leaf visually checked at PDF p. 3, First published 2010; hardback ISBN 9780521881050 and paperback 9780521707435. Preface pp. xi–xii read for the author’s account of changing the project from ocean geography toward law and sovereignty; acknowledgments are not an influence register. Core https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/search-for-sovereignty/1FCB3767F56B64879CF13618A139866A gives 30 November 2009 print release and 5 June 2014 online. Keep these distinct observations; the selected chronology uses the edition’s 2010 first-publication statement.

Read Benton’s answers on pirates/legal authorization and legal geography (printed pp. 75–76 and 78–79), and her final extended answer on anomalous legal zones and violence (pp. 82–83), using the publisher HTML and its PDF https://humanityjournal.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/2.1-Of-Pirates-Empire-and-Terror.pdf . PDF running footer explicitly says Spring 2011; the website’s 10 June 2014 post date is a later upload. Dan Edelstein’s answers and the editorial questions are distinguished from Benton’s. Her account of Agamben is a reported critique; Agamben’s books and the interview’s modern legal examples were not independently checked. This source supports historical-method claims, not present legal advice or a general verdict on postcolonial history. A direct local download of the PDF returned 403; the tool-rendered publisher PDF and full publisher HTML were readable.

Official publisher identifies both editors and July 2013 publication for paperback, hardback and ebook. Collection and introduction bodies unread in this packet. The joint introductory essay is also jointly credited in publisher-distributed contents, but conflicting chapter pagination is not adopted. This supports the publication event and editorial credit only.

Official publisher author/title, 22 April 2011 publication, ISBN 9780195393736 and description checked. Further comparative reading resource only; book body unread. Its corporate-sovereignty subject is related, but no transmission to or from Benton, direct reception, shared doctrine, or new historiographical relationship is established.

coauthorship_and_comparison_limits: Richard J. Ross is explicitly coeditor of the 2013 collection; no sole authorship of the volume is assigned to Benton.
Dan Edelstein is the other interviewee; his answers are not Benton’s. Humanity’s questions/editorial voice remain distinct.
Lisa Ford’s coauthorship of the separate Rage for Order is checked in the identity source but that unread book gets no new interpretive claim or dated event here.
Stern’s 2011 The Company-State is only a bibliography resource. No identity merge, author promotion or influence edge is accepted from its related subject.
